replying_to: Replying to Self-Supervision is All You Need for Solving Rubik's Cube
display_title: Official Review of Paper4191 by Reviewer DxXr

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper proposes to learn to solve the Rubik's cube using random paths starting from the goal state. At training time, the model learns to predict the last move (leading to the goal) given the initial state by optimising the cross-entropy loss. At test time, the probability over states is used to construct the path from the goal to the initial state using beam search. The method is applied to both DeepCube and Transform architectures, both of which are able to solve 100% of the randomly generated problems in the test set.
content.main_review:
### Strengths
- The method is simple and seems to work well with different types of architecture.
- The idea of showing that random paths starting from the goal state already produce strong cues for the optimal path is quite ingenious and, to the best of my knowledge, new.

### Weaknesses
- I am concerned by the lack of comparison against previous methods. It is not clear how Transformer-8L compares to DeepCube on solution length, solution optimality or computational complexity. Moreover, the authors claim their self-supervised method is more stable and robust than competing reinforcement learning methods but offer no evidence to support those claims.
- Even though the overall method seems simple, the paper is not easy to follow and it is not entirely clear to me how the method works at test time.
- The proposed method, albeit interesting, requires the solution to be known a priori. I believe this severely restricts its applicability, and for most combinatorial optimisation problems for which finding the optimal solution is not trivial, this approach would turn into an expensive supervised method rather than a self-supervised one.

### Questions
- It is not clear how the model works at test time. Could the authors explain further how the model is used at each step of the breadth-first search? 
- In a similar note, the inputs to the model are not entirely clear. How do the inputs vary at each step at inference time? Could the authors detail how they represent each state?
- Why construct the test set using only 100 scrambles, when previous methods [1, 2] used between 1K and 10K moves? Even though any state can be solved in 20 moves or less, that does not mean every instance generated with 20 random scrambles or more will be just as likely to be a hard instance (requiring 17 to 20 moves to solve). In other words, can we compare the results of this paper with the ones reported in [1,2] or are datasets generated with 1K scrambles in average harder than datasets generated with 100 scrambles?
- Do the authors have an interpretation to Figure 5? I could not distinguish a meaningful pattern in the attention mechanism.

### Minor issues
- The authors define their search procedure as breadth-first search with a 'maximum breadth' parameter. If I am not misinterpreting it, this method is more commonly referred to as beam search, which has beam size as a parameter.
- Given that the paper is much shorter than 9 pages, why not include the extra details and analyses from the appendix in the main text?

[1] Agostinelli, Forest, et al. "Solving the Rubik’s cube with deep reinforcement learning and search." Nature Machine Intelligence 1.8 (2019): 356-363.

[2] McAleer, Stephen, et al. "Solving the Rubik's Cube with Approximate Policy Iteration." International Conference on Learning Representations. 2018.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper has a valuable and promising insight. The authors show that random paths generated from the goal state are enough to train a model to solve the Rubik's cube using only cross-entropy loss, without resorting to reinforcement learning or hand-designed features. However, the exposition of the paper is unclear and feels incomplete, with many details left unexplained. More importantly, there is no direct comparisons with any other methods, which makes it hard to gauge what are the pros and cons of the proposed method.

content.title: Response to Reviewer DxXr
content.comment:
Thank you for providing a good review.

---

## Response to Criticisms

**The lack of comparison, expensiveness**

We have started a comparative evaluation with DeepCubeA and the optimal solver and will discuss strengths and weaknesses of the proposed method.

**Description of Inputs and inference, beam search**

Thank you for pointing these out. We will make changes.

## Questions	

**Why construct the test set using only 100 scrambles**

Because the diameter of Rubik’s Cube is 20 in half-turn metric, we assumed that 100 shuffling should be sufficient for random sampling from the state space, although we do not have a proof for this assumption. We are switching to test on the DeepCube dataset (1k~10k moves) you cited, which is available on GitHub.

**Do the authors have an interpretation to Figure 5?**

We found it interesting as an abstract representation of how intrinsically discrete pieces are processed by Transformers. Although we only mentioned *“[s]tarting with the [BUF] token attending to some corners and edges, the DNN produced cross-sectional token- and block-level associations with gradually distributed attention”*, this is the only observation we got.

## Other

**Note about the use of different architectures**

Because the comparison to existing methods is a priority and the use of Transformer is not at the core of our argument, we will only use the same architecture as DeepCubeA in the new version.

content.title: Rebuttal
content.comment:
I thank the authors for addressing my questions and for improving the quality of the paper considerably. In particular, the new experimental results give us a much more clear picture of the trade-offs of the proposed method.

I have a few comments regarding the new version of the paper.
- The description of the method is still not very easy to follow.
- I am a bit confused about the introduction of Assumption 2. It is reasonable to assume that the quality of the method depends on the quality of the scrambles generated during training, that is, of how far the training sequences are from the shortest path going from the last point to the goal. That means one would have to be careful not to generate training sequences that loop around a given state, for example, but I do not see why the specific requirement of knowing God's number. Could the authors expand on that?
- The new experimental results indicate the proposed method does not outperform the baselines. That is fine in principle—not every contribution needs to be about improving the state-of-the-art—but the authors could expand the discussion on the benefits or insights we can derive from their approach. It is clear their method is simple and intuitive, which is a positive aspect, but there are other angles that are not fully considered and could benefit the paper.
     - Is the model more efficient than competing methods? Figure 4 shows us running times, but there is almost no discussion on which conclusions we get from this experiment.
     - Can the proposed method be combined with other approaches, e.g. imitation learning? How and why?
     - Is there any particular insight that could benefit the combinatorial optimisation or machine learning communities?

display_title: Thank you Reviewer DxXr for your response

content.title: Thank you Reviewer DxXr for your response
content.comment:
Thanks a lot for your comment. 

We will try to improve it until the last minute, based on your suggestions, questions, and concerns.

---


## I do not see why the specific requirement of knowing God's number
In our method, “training sequences that loop around a given state” are not necessarily prohibited; after all, some random paths are inevitably sub-optimal, meaning that they can be compressed into shorter sequences of moves.
God’s number or its upper bound should be known, but not for the quality of random moves, which you cannot control. Rather, we want to know it for two reasons: 

1. To explore its state space of all distances, and 

2. To avoid making predictions that are scrambled above the maximum complexity. 

The first should be obvious. As for the second, when you apply additional moves to the furthest state, a DNN cannot make good predictions on the state, because probability distributions of random moves would be biased to both goal state and further state. 

Probably the mistake we made is the word “redundant” because it can mean “non-optimal”, but we intended to mean “scrambles exceeding the maximum complexity. We will revise this section. 




## [T]he proposed method does not outperform the baselines. That is fine in principle—...

One thing we want to inform of you is that the inferior result of our experiment is attributed to lesser computation in both training and inference, and there still is a potential for surpassing the baselines. However, because our purpose is not to make it a SOTA and we do not have so much computing resources, we only demonstrate its simplicity, stability, and scalability.




## Is the model more efficient than competing methods? Figure 4 shows us running times, but there is almost no discussion on which conclusions we get from this experiment.

In the Discussion section, we talk about the amount of computation and scalability of the method. However, we do not want to make a comparison in terms of computation time. This is because, while our method can run faster than DeepCubeA and the optimal solver, it is not a fair comparison. With limited beam widths in our experiment, the DNN did not expand as many nodes as the other two during a search. Thus, we do not discuss if our method is more efficient or faster, and we only say that our method is scalable with the amount of training and inference computation.

We will add a note about this in the Discussion.



## Can the proposed method be combined with other approaches, e.g. imitation learning? How and why?

We have a few shallow ideas that are not validated.

Our method could be potentially used as pre-training for further optimization with reinforcement learning. The “policy” a DNN learns in our method is blurred by the randomness of training, which RL could potentially rectify. This probably cannot be considered “imitation learning”, but should give a stable guideline for an RL agent.

Another thing would be to apply our method to problems of continuous action space if possible. For example, when the task for a robot finger is to touch a button, starting with the finger touching the button (goal state), we may first apply random inverse moves based on a continuous probability distribution.

We will consider adding this to Discussion. However, we may choose not to.



## Is there any particular insight that could benefit the combinatorial optimisation or machine learning communities?

We show a very simple and inexpensive method for solving a specific class of problems with high optimality in comparison to existing methods. 

For combinatorial optimization, there might be other problems with undiscovered nature like this. Alternatively, the proposed method could extend with fewer constraints. This work demonstrates a new example of self-supervised feature learning, which is a hot topic in machine learning, especially natural language processing and computer vision.

---

Just one last time, thank you for reviewing our paper. You are not the only peer reviewer, but your feedback certainly made our paper visibly better.

Once again I thank the authors for attending to my comments and questions. The new version of the paper is a much more solid submission, so I revised my score accordingly. However, I still have two main concerns about the paper.

For those reasons, I still think the paper is short of the acceptance criteria but am open to change my mind during the remaining of the reviewing process.

content.title: Response to Rebuttal (2)
content.comment:
We truly appreciate your feedback. Although the latest version reflects your suggestions, we will try to clarify the remaining concerns to our best.

---

### 1. Relevance to combinatorial optimisation

We must admit that the proposed method has some constraints, as far as we can empirically show at the moment.  It is just interesting.

Most importantly, as you mentioned, a target problem **must** have a known goal state (we would not call it an optimal *state* since optimality is determined not by state but path in our case). Accordingly, potential applications are quite limited within the field of combinatorial optimisation, at least now.

However, as we discussed in the final version (taking into account your last comment), our method has prospects for a broader range of applications, possibly with fewer constraints. For example, our method might be useful for problems with a continuous action space / variable distances (e.g., routing); else, as a stable pretraining method for reinforcement learning (e.g., teaching a robot to press a button). With such potential extensions, our method could be useful for problems whose objective is to reach a certain state. 

### 2. Discussion underdeveloped

**Methodology still unclear**

We drastically updated sections **Experiment > Rubik’s Cube** and  **Proposed Method > Inference**. We believe that they are much clearer now and that these sections need no figure or pseudocode. If still unclear, would you mind telling us what is not well explained yet?

**Discussion**

Additionally to the comparative optimality and the scalability of our method, we also explain the trade-off between inference time and optimality. Other than that, we could not gain any further insights from our experimental results. Also, because we have presented all we know about our method in **Proposed Method**, we have stuck to discussing potential applications and extensions in the Discussion. 

---

Even if you do not change your recommendation anymore, we sincerely welcome additional feedback or recommendations. Thank you so much for your time and effort in reviewing our work.

content.main_review:
The contribution is that it is shown that self supervised learning may be enough to solve some rubik's cube instances close to optimally.
Rubik's cube is a combinatorial problem, and as such a planning approach would be better suited instead of a neural network. It would be interesting to hear why the author's chose to apply a neural network instead. The use of transformers is an interesting approach, although also a breadth first search is used.
Deeper questions, comparing planning to a neural network, such as how the history is encoded in the network, are not addressed.
The paper does not explain clearly enough how the network is able to perform planning to optimality, and unclear is how this approach could solve a full problem.
It is unclear how this method could be applied if there is no goal. 
The paper states that RL is the main method for solving rubik's cube, however, combinatorial search methods are used more often and to greater success.

Related work with respect to model-based end-to-end planning by neural networks, such as Value Iteration Networks, Predictron, and MuZero is missing.

The paper claims to be better than RL, however no comparison is performed.

The work is interesting, but needs to be developed further, and applied more fully to more applications.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4191 by Reviewer rL6t

content.title: Response to Reviewer rL6t
content.comment:
We appreciate your excellent review and apologize for the delayed response.

First and foremost, we wanted and developed a simple and stable method for combinatorial puzzles with a predefined goal.

As we argue in the introduction, employing a logical search algorithm requires detailed knowledge about a target problem. In the case of Rubik's Cube, we need to know about group theory, and also need a pattern database, for which DeepCubeA researchers needed 182GB memory in order to run in a reasonable time. 

Alternatively, we could choose to apply end-to-end planning methods like reinforcement learning for automatic heuristic search, as you mentioned. However, they are hard to build and often unstable. Among the list of RL methods you presented, Predictron might be suited for goal-predefined combinatorial problems on implicit graphs. However, to our knowledge, there has been no study applying Predictron to implicit planning problems like Rubik's Cube and 15 puzzle. Furthermore, we believe that model-based end-to-end planning is not well suited for implicit planning tasks largely because millions of nodes need to be expanded for finding a goal and getting rewarded for an episode. On the other hand, deep approximate value iteration like DeepCubeA and our stepwise learning method are better suited for the class of problem.

As for VIN and MuZero, they are not within the scope of the present study. VIN is for *explicit* path planning, and MuZero is characterized by the internalization of environmental lookahead for learning rules. Our future work may focus on path planning on an explicit graph or possibly environmental lookahead for speed up and generalization, but at this point, we do not consider either of them.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a self-supervised method for learning to solve Rubik's cube instances. The method relies on randomly perturbing a solved Rubik's cube and training a neural network to predict the last move that led to the perturbed state. The experiments show that a self-supervised Transformer combined with breadth-first-search can successfully solve randomly scrambled Rubik's cubes.
content.main_review:
## Strengths
- The proposed approach is rather simple and intuitive.
- Results indicate that the method works. 
- Appears to be easy and stable to train.
- The authors are upfront about the assumptions that the proposed method relies on.

## Criticism and comments
1) There are sentences that need to be reworded/rewritten to improve clarity.
Examples:
"Assuming that the first move in a random path is probabilistically most likely optimal". How is the "first move" defined? From goal to scramble, or the other way around? Later it is clarified from the context, but at this point in the paper, this is rather confusing.
"At all nodes, convoluting the probabilities of all the possible paths, a move in more optimal
paths turns out to have a higher probability of being in the unknown path." (caption of figure 1)
What do the authors mean by "convoluting the probabilities of all the possible paths"? Furthermore, the notation could be improved. For example, the probability of taking a particular move (which one?) as the first step to a specific target node in a path of n moves or more is denoted $p_n$. Specific notation for target and starting nodes, as well as precise notation for the $i$-th move would help clarify the math. Another example is equation (1) where the sum is not indexed. Again, the meaning could be inferred from the context, but this hinders the readability of the text. Another issue is that various details are missing from the paper.
For example, the precise inputs to the DNN are not described, so it's not clear how the problem instances are actually encoded. We are given the sentence:
"As input into DNNs, the edges and the corners have 48 unique possible states, determined by their spatial locations and
flip/twist states 1" which is qualitatively informative, but not sufficient.
A section/paragraph that clearly describes the input, how it is processed and how are states encoded as well as how a solution is obtained and represented would help improve clarity.
Furthermore, the text assumes a certain level of familiarity with Rubik's cube solving. A paragraph that describes the problem and explains the different states and moves would be helpful to make the text self-contained.


2) This approach relies on two key premises. First, that the goal state of the problem is known. Granted that premise, then optimal moves are assumed to be more frequent.  The authors claim for (3) "...and just taking a sub-optimal (alternative) move should not largely increase the total number of same-distance paths. Therefore, we assume that this holds true to varying degrees depending on the problem being addressed." However, explicit proofs are not provided, or even specific constructions/examples for other problems.
Since the "Contributions" paragraph claims that this is applicable to combinatorial problems with a known goal state, more thorough arguments and experiments are required to establish this. Otherwise, the scope of this work appears to be limited to essentially learning based on a heuristic for a single problem.

3) From the experimental section it is not exactly clear whether the comparison is with the original DeepCube setup or with just a DeepCube architecture trained with self-supervision. Given the training curves, I have to assume that it is a DeepCube architecture trained in the same self-supervised way. It would be good to experimentally show exactly how this approach compares to other Rubik's cube approaches in the literature (solvers and NNs). Are there benefits in time complexity for either training or evaluation? Is training more stable? Those would have to be thoroughly demonstrated to provide support for the proposed method (see for example the paper by Agostinelli et al. that you are citing)
content.summary_of_the_review:
While the proposed method proposes an interesting trick for the solution of Rubik's cubes with self-supervision, it does not provide sufficient theoretical or experimental backup for its claimed contribution. The experiments show that it works, but there is not enough evidence to support the claimed general applicability of this technique beyond Rubik's cube solving. Furthermore, even within the context of the Rubik's cube problem, the authors did not provide sufficient experiments that establish the benefits of this work over related work. Therefore, apart from the simplicity of the approach (which is good), the potential impact of this work appears to be rather limited.

Update: I have updated my score based on the authors' modifications to the paper. The authors have shown that this technique can work on an additional problem and achieve competitive results. Given that in terms of performance this method does not particularly stand out (partly because of computational budget reasons), the authors would either have to establish its broader applicability to other combinatorial problems and puzzles and/or provide a more thorough investigation of the idea. Could the model improve by predicting multiple moves ahead instead of just one using the same principle? Instead of random scrambles, could they be biased? (maybe based on some property of the problem). Developing the idea and perhaps connecting it with the literature in a meaningful way could make the contribution of the paper more relevant for a larger part of the (combinatorial) ML community. As it stands, its main appeal is simplicity which while definitely appreciated, is not enough.

content.title: Response to Reviewer vZZv
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our work. We particularly appreciate valuable suggestions. 

---

## Clarity, definition, math expressions, etc.
We evaluated your criticisms/suggestions to be valid, so the new version will reflect changes based on them. As for the representation of Rubik’s Cube, we switched to the conventional sticker color representation, abandoning the control by “spatial locations and flip/twist states,” which was probably the most confusing thing. Still, we will incorporate more on how a DNN takes Rubik’s Cube and how solutions are obtained by beam search.

## No explicit proofs for Assumption 1
If I understood your point correctly, you are pointing at the lack of proof for doubting the generalizability of the method. However, the degree to which Assumption 1 applies to a specific problem does not interfere with Condition 1. If less optimal paths are learned more probable than more optimal paths, meaning that Assumption 1 is violated, a trained DNN will more likely go backward through the suboptimal paths at inference, following peaks of a probability distribution at each inference step. The assumption is only relevant to the optimality of models trained with the proposed method.

As for explicit proofs of Assumption 1, it is impossible (or extremely hard) to provide proof. You will need a lot of computation for problems on implicit graphs (e. g., Rubik’s Cube), while You can easily create a set of paths violating Assumption 1 on a small explicit graph (e. g., by arbitrarily creating/pruning specific edges). 

## Comparison
We agree that comparison is necessary for the evaluation of our method. And you are right, we only compared the “architecture” of DeepCube, not methods (RL). Given your feedback, we started working on re-running the experiment and evaluating the method on DeepCubeA dataset.

display_title: Official Review of Paper4191 by Reviewer RsVr

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes learning to solve the Rubik's cube by randomly scrambling the cube and using a deep neural network to predict the random actions. The authors argue that, if optimal actions are more likely than random ones, that this method will be biased towards finding optimal solutions. When searching for a solution, the network predicts an action and the opposite action is taken, as the network predicts actions taken when scrambling from the solved state and now wants to return to the solved state.

When solving a cube, the authors use beam search and keep states based on the move probability. They experiment with keeping 10, 100, and 1000 states at each depth in the beam search. The authors use a dataset of 1000 cubes scrambled 100 times to test their method. The results show that, as the number of states keeping more states during beam search leads to shorter paths with the shortest average path being 20.5.
content.main_review:
Strengths:

The authors propose a method that only relies on a random sequence of random reverse moves. This assumes access to both a forward model (for solving) and a backward model, for starting from the goal and generating random moves. Given a fixed dataset, the time taken to train does not depend on the size of the action space as it does with approximate value iteration. While Q-learning mitigates this problem, if the argument about the assumption of optimal actions is valid, then this method does not need to worry about exploring different actions as Q-learning does.

Weaknesses:

The evaluation is poor and useful data from related work that is freely available is not used.

The search algorithm proposed, beam search, which the authors call "breadth-first search", is not complete. Meaning that, if there is a solution, it is not guaranteed to find it. This is because a finite number of states are kept at every iteration. On the other hand, A* search, which was used in related work [1], is a complete algorithm.

How much this theoretical property of completeness matters in this application cannot be clearly evaluated as the authors evaluate on cubes only scrambled 100 times while the latest work uses cubes scrambled 1,000 to 10,000 times [1]. Since the authors do not compute the cost of a shortest path, we cannot be sure how close their method comes to finding one. However, the dataset which contains the states scrambled 1,000 to 10,000 times along with the cost of a shortest path is freely available [2,3]. However, the authors do not use it here. Perhaps this is because the authors use a slightly different action space. Nonetheless, the code used to compute a shortest path for this action space is also freely available [4].

The authors erroneously claim "Since an estimated 98% of all possible states take 17–20 moves to be solved at shortest (Rokicki et al., 2014), the trained DNN can be considered a near-optimal solver as hypothesized, even before full convergence in training and with a compromised search algorithm." They sampled states by scrambling the cube 100 times which is not the same as randomly sampling states from the state space.

Another shortcoming of the evaluation is the authors do not say how much time their method took to find a solution. On a related note, what is the average depth of the beam search?

In summary, to understand if what the authors are proposing is practical in this case, the authors should test this method on data where the cost of a shortest path can be computed so that we can understand how complex the solutions they are finding actually are. I would recommend using states scrambled between 1,000 and 10,000 times, as in related work. This can help us understand if the lack of completeness of beam search is even a factor. To make results even more convincing, the authors can use the few states of the Rubik's cube that are known to have the longest shortest path possible (i.e. the "superflip" [5]). Furthermore, the time the method takes should also be reported.

Other comments:

I do not understand equation one. Why would the probability of an action at timestep i be conditioned on the action at timestep i+1? How does the present depend on the future?

References:
[1] Agostinelli, Forest, et al. "Solving the Rubik’s cube with deep reinforcement learning and search." Nature Machine Intelligence 1.8 (2019): 356-363.
[2] https://codeocean.com/capsule/5723040/tree/v1
[3] https://github.com/forestagostinelli/DeepCubeA
[4] https://github.com/rokicki/cube20src
[5] https://cube20.org/
content.summary_of_the_review:
The authors propose an algorithm that could be potentially useful in specific settings where random reverse actions are likely to be optimal. However, the evaluation of the method is poor and differs significantly from related work in terms of difficulty and evaluation metrics. 

### AFTER AUTHOR FEEDBACK ###
The authors have incorporated many of my suggestions and now show that their method can solve all Rubik's cube and 15-puzzle test states using their method. Though the results are not as good as DeepCubeA, it is quite unexpected that this simple approach works at all. It is essentially: imitation learning of a noisy teacher (the last move taken when scrambling) followed by beam search. The simplicity of this method could be useful in environments where exploration becomes difficult, therefore, I am increasing my score from a 3 to a 5. 

One aspect that is still lacking is an analysis of this beam search method. For example, though no cost-to-go function is learned, does this method approximately try to minimize the cost-to-go function while searching? The cost-to-go function DeepCubeA learns can also be used to induce a policy (i.e. a softmax based on the cost-to-go) and then be used in this beam search, which one performs better? Is Is the combination of beam search and self-supervised learning objective important or can a policy induced from a cost-to-go function also be used?

content.title: Response to Reviewer RsVr
content.comment:
Thank you for reviewing our work and providing critical points.

---

## The lack of comparative evaluation
We are convinced about the lack of comparison. We were naive to believe that a demonstration of Rubik’s Cube alone should make a sufficient contribution, when a comparison to existing methods is certainly essential to our research. As you guessed right, we skipped it because we originally developed the proposed method for half-turn metrics while DeepCubeA employs quarter-turn metrics. As for 100-move scrambles, we simply expected it to be enough for random sampling, considering that a path of 20 moves or fewer can connect any two states.

After reading your review and careful consideration, we decided to compare our method to the existing ones on solution lengths, number of nodes, and time taken to reach the goal, using the DeepCubeA dataset you presented.


## About Equation 1.

We intended to mean that the learned probability distributions of future moves at inference time should approximate those of random moves, which in turn be past moves during training. In other words, probabilities are not actually dependent on future moves, but they are hypothesized to approximate probabilities of past training moves . We could not come up with better expressions, but will work on disambiguation.

content.title: Response to AFTER AUTHOR FEEDBACK
content.comment:
First, thank you for excellent suggestions, and also for changing the score after the updates.

---

## Performance (vs. DeepCubeA)

As we mentioned in the Discussion, we believe that the performance inferiority is largely due to the amount of computation. As Figure 3 depicts, **our method is scalable** with both training and inference computation. Thus, with more training steps and wider beam search, **it could potentially be as good as DeepCubeA**.

## Beam search analysis

If we understood correctly, you are pointing out the use of a search algorithm different from that of DeepCubeA. We use the simple beam search, whereas DeepCubeA used the batch weighted A* search (BWAS).

As you say, it was possible to test the DeepCubeA policy network with the same beam search. However, we have two reasons not to: 

1. We can assume that the best result is reported for DeepCubeA, thus using a different search algorithm could result in a worse result, making a comparison unfair.
2. They reported that the cost-to-go coefficient λ=0.6 resulted in the best result and lower λ resulted in longer solutions [1], implying that the use of the cost-to-go function is better for DeepCubeA, although this is shown true only with BWAS.

Also, because we are not studying DeepCubeA itself, we want to stick to the simplicity of method and comparison. Regarding the minimization of cost-to-go, it feels intuitive that the cost-to-go, as a metric like accuracy, would decrease as the DNN continues a search in our method as it gets closer to the goal.


---

[1] Agostinelli, Forest, et al. "Solving the Rubik’s cube with deep reinforcement learning and search." Nature Machine Intelligence 1.8 (2019): 356-363.

---

## About Superflip testing

Also, after consideration, we decided not to conduct the test on the furthest states (three *superflip plus fourspot* cases) you initially suggested.
This is because such an analysis would not provide a statistically meaningful result. The result would largely depend on chance (i. g., if the furthest states or similar appear during training) and calculation time (with only three states, we could use a very wide beam search).

content.title: Before Discussion Stage 1 Ends
content.comment:
First of all, we appreciate your excellent reviews. Although it took us a couple of days to take the low scores head on, we generally agree with your points and consider them essential to our study.

We are also re-experimenting and re-writing claims based on it. This is taking a lot of time, and we expect it to take another day or two to upload the next version. Therefore, before we shift from Discussion Stage 1 to 2, we would like to inform you of what will change according to your suggestions in advance.

---

## A theoretical modification

We have noticed another limitation of the proposed method: 

For efficient training and inference, the maximum number of moves necessary to solve a problem (God’s number), or at least its upper bound, must be known. 

 In the proposed method, let $N$ be God’s number for a specific problem, a DNN receives problem states scrambled for $1$~$N$ moves. If we estimate the number larger than it actually is, the DNN will have more unnecessarily redundant scrambles in training. On the other hand, if you underestimate $N$, then the DNN would not well adapt to problem states of higher complexities during inference. This further limits the generalizability of the proposed method.

## Experimental modifications
1. We will re-run the experiment and compare our results to those of DeepCubeA and the optimal solver [1], which are available on GitHub [2]. There are two main metrics to compare: solution length and calculation time. Calculation time is highly dependent on hardware and code, making the direct comparison very difficult. However, when using a DNN, the number of nodes is highly proportional to calculation time, as it sees almost all nodes expanded during a search. We utilize this feature to compare our method to DeepCubeA, controlling for per-node calculation time. It might be confusing to describe both the actual time taken in our environment and the normalized time, but we thought it was necessary for a fair comparison. Also, for a fair comparison, we switch to the quarter-turn metric (90-degree) and sticker-wise representations of Rubik’s Cube, abandoning the half-turn metric and the piecewise representation.


2. In addition to this, we examine how accuracy and speed scale with the maximum width of the beam search. A clear fact is that the wider the search, the slower and shorter solutions will be; the narrower, the faster and longer solutions. However, with a fixed maximum width, we cannot make a clear comparison with existing methods. Therefore, we obtain a 2D map of solution length and calculation time to see how our method positions with respect to DeepCubeA and the optimal solver depending on this parameter.


3. We are doing the same experiment for the 15-puzzle. As with Rubik's Cube, God's number is known and both DeepCube and Optimal solutions are provided [1]. For the sake of conciseness and comprehensibility, we would like to focus the spotlight on Rubik's Cube exclusively in the main text and give 15-puzzle in Appendix as another application example. However, it is also an option to discuss it in parallel with Rubik's Cube for supporting the generalizability of the proposed method.


We will soon upload the new version. However, if you have any suggestions/questions about these upcoming changes, please do not hesitate to comment even before that.


> [1] Agostinelli, Forest, et al. "Solving the Rubik’s cube with deep reinforcement learning and search." Nature Machine Intelligence 1.8 (2019): 356-363. 

> [2] https://github.com/forestagostinelli/DeepCubeA
